cards.relevant: 事件暴露了RSPO认证体系在实际执行中的漏洞——即使是被认证为可持续的种植园，其内部的高保护价值区域仍未能免受火灾威胁，引发对棕榈油行业监管有效性的质疑。
cards.context: 印尼油棕种植园常通过焚烧方式清理土地，导致周边泥炭地森林频繁起火。此次火灾发生在声称符合可持续标准的种植园内，说明认证机制可能未能有效防止火灾对濒危物种栖息地的破坏。

cards.source_text: - Conservationists are racing to rescue orangutans from fire-affected habitat inside an Indonesian oil palm concession. - Some orangutans have been brought to safety, while others are believed to remain in the area. - First Resources, which owns the concession, says it enforces a strict “zero-burning policy” across all planting activities. - Another, larger conservation area that once supported an estimated 200 orangutans has also been affected by fire. JAKARTA — Conservationists are racing to rescue orangutans from a fire-ravaged peat-swamp forest inside an RSPO-certified oil palm concession in West Kalimantan, with smoke still rising and the ground remaining dangerously hot. The 657-hectare (1,623-acre) forest, designated as a High Conservation Value (HCV) area inside PT Kayung Agro Lestari (KAL), is home to around 60 Bornean orangutans (Pongo pygmaeus), one of three orangutan species in the world and the only one found on the island of Borneo, according to conservationists. The forest was also used in October 2015 to release four orangutans rescued by the Yayasan International Animal Rescue Indonesia (YIARI), a Borneo-based NGO working to establish and maintain sustainable orangutan populations. Nearly 11 years after four orangutans were released there, the peat-swamp forest that provided their habitat has itself been almost completely affected by fire, according to satellite analysis by technology consultancy TheTreeMap. The analysis indicates that one of the major fires began on Aug. 8 along a canal at the edge of the oil palm plantation in Ketapang district, before spreading westward into the HCV forest. Conservationists are working to rescue orangutans still believed to be in the area. Some animals have already been brought to safety, while others are believed to remain in the affected forest. The rescue effort has been complicated by the condition of the forest, where fallen tree trunks, lingering smoke and dangerously hot ground make movement difficult. Peat fires can continue burning beneath the surface even after flames are no longer visible, creating additional risks for both orangutans and rescuers. How many orangutans are left? The exact number of orangutans that occupied the affected forest before the fires, and how many have survived, remains unclear. cards.source_text: It sounds like a Disney movie: three wild dogs, all brothers, on an epic journey to find a home of their own after their family tells them to leave. They dodge cars and hunters in search of a new life, navigating bushmeat snares and the hostility of a human-dominated landscape until they find a new haven on the African savannah. But this is exactly what happened in Zambia last year, when three endangered African wild dogs made the longest-ever recorded single journey of any mammal from the continent. The brothers travelled more than 2,500 miles (4,100km) over eight months in their “dispersal” – when a young dog comes of age and must establish new territory to find a mate and start a family of their own. From point to point, starting in Kafue national park in western Zambia to their final destination in the Luangwa valley in the east of the country, the brothers covered 340 miles (546km), which is also a record. The epic single journey is almost equivalent to travelling the length of Chile by foot and farther than the famous wildebeest and zebra migration across the Serengeti in east Africa. The previous record was 2,418 miles, also made by African wild dogs, which moved between Loliondo, in northern Tanzania’s Ngorongoro district, and Tsavo West national park in southern Kenya in 2012. Dr Matt Becker, chief executive of the Zambian Carnivore Programme (ZCP), whose scientists were monitoring the wild dogs and have published their findings in the journal Ecology, says: “These extraordinary journeys show that natural connections between Africa’s wildlife strongholds still exist. But they also reveal how difficult and dangerous those journeys have become. “Rather than relying solely on fenced protected areas, these findings reinforce the value of investing in connected landscapes. The dogs are showing us that connectivity still works; now we need to do more to protect and strengthen it.” The researchers tracked 19 separate groups of wild dogs to monitor their dispersals, including a group of sisters to the three brothers who were far less successful at finding a new range. Two of the sisters died, probably caught in snares, but not before they had a touching final encounter with their siblings. Two months into their journey, the group of brothers and sisters came across each other deep in Zambia’s copper-belt mining region, spending the day together before going their separate ways again. cards.source_text: Bonnie Greer personified courage, humour, principle and generosity. Before knowing her in person, I met her work. Her 1994 debut novel Hanging by Her Teeth – about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father – was sent to me for endorsement by its publisher, and I commented unhesitatingly: “Writing with sharpness, wit and poignancy, Bonnie Greer gathers the sequestered memories behind one Black woman’s bitter-sweet blues.” The scope of Bonnie’s own life is beyond anything fictional, encompassing highs and lows, triumphs and challenges, her trajectory starting in the West Side of Chicago and ending up navigating iconic areas of London – whether Holland Park or Covent Garden or Soho – as if to the manor born. It was an honour to become her friend, sharing many a good time, offering a consoling shoulder if needed. An added bonus was to meet her husband David Hutchins. What a wonderful mutually supportive team they made. Bonnie’s activism marched side by side with her creativity and powers of persuasion. Friendship, support, empathy and behind-the-scenes involvement were all part of who she was. She could be effervescently sociable. There was an era when she relished get-togethers of a sort of ladies-who-lunch club that she would organise, where we might chat for hours, exchanging memories, planning dreamy never-to-be-fulfilled projects. I recall one gathering that took place at the House of Commons – with Diane Abbott, Verna Wilkins, Maya Jaggi and Nana Ayebia Clarke – when Bonnie suddenly made us all pause to reflect on the fact we were all sitting there, with a view of the Thames and London’s landscape, given where we had come from. Seemingly ready to re-invent herself, she was perhaps defying anyone to easily label her. She could be public intellectual, television pundit, dramatist, librettist, academic. Her repertoire was wide-ranging and ever-expanding, with fresh ideas emerging at every opportunity. She fearlessly spoke out, forged new connections, took on weighty burdens. She lent expertise to numerous national cultural institutions – including on the boards of the British Museum, the Royal Opera House and the London Film School, and as vice president of the Shaw Society and chancellor of Kingston University London. cards.summary: 2025年7月在澳大利亚黄金海岸附近，一头座头鲸被拍到反复返回其死产幼崽所在位置超过一小时。格里菲斯大学和海洋世界基金会的最新报告认为，这是首次记录的须鲸母亲照料死亡新生幼崽的案例。研究人员谨慎地使用"死后关注行为"而非"哀悼"来描述这一行为。

cards.social_impact: 该视频引发公众对鲸类情感能力的关注和讨论，研究者强调不能直接以人类情感衡量动物行为，但此类观察有助于推动动物福利和海洋保护政策。
cards.source_text: Humpback whale filmed apparently grieving its stillborn calf – video。Footage recorded in July 2025 shows a humpback whale repeatedly returning for more than an hour to the spot where its stillborn calf lay, a kilometre off Australia’s Gold Coast. While similar behaviours have been documented in pilot whales, dolphins and killer whales, a new report from Griffith University and the Sea World Foundation suggests this is the first described case of a toothless baleen whale mother caring for her deceased newborn calf. ‘However, we can’t directly measure the emotional state of whales,’ writes Olaf Meynecke, a co-author of the report. ‘The behaviours we observed could represent grief, but they could also reflect maternal attachment, confusion or instinctive caregiving. For this reason, researchers use broader terms – such as postmortem attentive behaviour – rather than concluding that whales grieve in the human sense’ Do whales grieve? cards.source_text: - The African dwarf crocodile is found in dense swamps and flooded forests across large parts of West and Central Africa. - Experts say these reptiles, which are widely hunted and sold, are under pressure from overexploitation and loss of habitat. - A recently published study set out to assess how many of the reptiles were sold in three bushmeat markets in the Niger Delta. The African dwarf crocodile is the world’s smallest living crocodile. These reptiles, nocturnal predators of crabs, gastropods and the occasional fish or small mammal, can reach 2 meters (6.6 feet) in length. They are found in dense swamps and flooded forests across large parts of West and Central Africa. Despite being listed as vulnerable on the IUCN’s Red List, the African dwarf crocodile (Osteolaemus tetraspis) has not been assessed by the conservation organization for 30 years. Anecdotal evidence suggests the crocodile’s numbers have declined sharply in many places where they were formerly common due to over-harvesting and destruction of their habitat. “The dwarf crocodile is particularly well-suited for the commercial trade,” ecologist Mitchell Eaton wrote in 2008. “Its small size and slow metabolism allow it to be captured and transported live over long distances without the need for refrigeration.” These unfortunately convenient characteristics have made the species a prized target for hunters across the reptiles’ range and conservationists fear this is putting crocodile populations under unsustainable pressure. For a study published in August in the journal BMC Zoology, conservation biologist Israel Ogorode and colleagues surveyed sales of African dwarf crocodiles at three markets in the Niger Delta, aiming to collect data about how many of the reptiles are sold — and who is doing the selling. Ogorode and the researchers visited three bushmeat markets in the Niger Delta region — Edumanon, Ogbe-Ijaw and Uwa — every other week between October 2021 and April 2022 to count the number of crocodiles for sale, randomly selecting 30 vendors at each site for their survey. In six months, the researchers recorded 158 crocodiles, roughly 80% of these were young or fully grown adults, while around 20% were juveniles less than 60 centimeters (24 inches) long. Despite the small sample size, the researchers hypothesize that hunting for crocodiles is easier during the dry season, between October and February. cards.source_text: - The return of a giant anteater to the protected area in the humid Gran Chaco in Argentina has given researchers hope that ecosystem restoration could help restore biodiversity in an area threatened by habitat loss and agriculture. - Passive restoration in the area meant removing pressures on the landscape from livestock, dogs, hunting, and fishing, which allowed the natural vegetation to recover. - Experts say it’s too early to say if the anteater’s return is the start of the species’ recovery or just a one-off, and call for continuous monitoring. In 2025, a giant anteater returned to the Alma Guaraní reserve in Argentina’s Corrientes province. It marked the first sighting of this vulnerable and emblematic mammal in the region since 1986. That return is believed to be the result of restoration work that began in the reserve in 2021, according to a paper published in Restoration Ecology, which makes the case that passive restoration in particular may have triggered the species’ return to the area. “It was the first register of the giant anteater in 40 years in Corrientes province, and it was spontaneous,” said co-author Rosario Montiel, from the National University of the Northeast and CEO of climate and environmental startup RestoreData. “We think that in this area, in this reserve, this animal has found food and all its needs to settle there.” It’s not known where the giant anteater came from. Montiel and colleagues suggest the individual, thought to be a male, may have crossed over from neighboring Chaco province, swimming across the nearby Parana River when water levels hit a historical low in 2024. Giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla) are classified as vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. Habitat loss is a major threat, driven primarily by the expansion of agriculture and livestock ranching, and is behind much of the species’ decline across Argentina and the wider Gran Chaco region. Infrastructure development, such as increasing road networks, and hunting are also significant threats. Anteaters are caught for the pet trade and accidentally killed by hunters’ dogs. cards.source_text: In his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schubert’s favourite pupils. This, Wittgenstein argues, was a totally understandable act of grief. He goes on to suggest, however, that if, in his grief, Schubert’s brother had left the scores untouched, or even burned them, then that too would be equally legible to us. Such is the disorienting nature of loss – in its wake, anything goes. In The Strangers, Women’s prize-winning author Naomi Alderman tests this thesis to its limits. How about dealing with grief by writing an uneasy memoir/speculative fiction hybrid about the sudden appearance of a new species of quasi-badgers that seem to improve the quality of local soil? Well, it turns out Wittgenstein was right. The Strangers, despite (or perhaps because of) its many ragged idiosyncrasies, is a remarkably successful evocation of loss. Narrated by “the novelist Naomi Alderman”, who is mourning both her recently deceased mother and a series of failed pregnancies, the book ranges incisively across the vast affective terrain bequeathed to those who go on living: despair, disorientation, solipsism, petulance, regret, resignation … the list goes on. After all, grief is not an emotion – it is all the emotions, all at once. And by braiding the memoir within a subtly unnerving tale of eco-horror infestation, Alderman substantially raises the philosophical and symbolic stakes. It is a high-risk, sporadically successful manoeuvre, but one that recognises the gravity of the task at hand. In the same way that a gravestone is an attempt to give form to an absence, Alderman’s structural ingenuity allows the reader to wrangle some of the ineffable aspects of grief into something more coherent and bounded. The plot itself is simple enough, and relatively small fry compared to some of Alderman’s previous work, such as thwarting the techno-apocalypse (The Future) or upending the global gender hierarchy (The Power). Twenty-five years on, Marriott fears smartphones have all but killed reading for everyone. He had to get rid of his own – “George Eliot is no match” – and now, watching the rest of us scroll, he worries not only that we will lose the ability to appreciate Middlemarch, but that we risk falling prey to tyrants and anti-vaxxers forging “a world very different to the one we have known … mystical, tribal and autocratic”. But the conservation charity English Heritage is recruiting a team of volunteer scythers to maintain 21st-century meadowland in the old-fashioned way. The first scythers have been trained and will use their new skills in the meadows around an abbey in Somerset, where it is hoped that as well as helping to keep the age-old practice alive, they will protect a rare type of bumblebee. Ginny Slade, who has completed the training, said she found there was something therapeutic about scything. “You need a level of physical fitness but it’s also about enthusiasm and the passion to learn heritage skills,” she said. “It’s a repetitive movement. You find your rhythm and zone into it. You can really connect with the meadow, the landscape.” The first volunteers have also found that using the scythe is something of a sensual treat – the sound of the blade cutting, the scent of the meadow. Slade said: “Scything is a wonderful example of how traditional skills can still have a role in addressing modern challenges. We hope to help create the diverse, flower-rich habitats that pollinators need while also preserving knowledge and skills that have shaped our landscapes.” Slade, a volunteer and community engagement manager with English Heritage, is one of the first to be trained by professionals at the Exmoor National Park Authority in the art of using and maintaining a scythe. “You want a really good scythe,” said Slade. “If you look after them, they can last generations.” English Heritage rewards volunteers with bread and cheese (it also thought about providing West Country cider but thought this was not a good idea on health and safety grounds). cards.source_text: It’s an ungainly word for English speakers, which is maybe why we do not hear it often: Gleichschaltung. Yet the concept remains central for a clear view of what happened to Germany in the 1930s. In 1933, the nation completely transformed, seemingly overnight, through “a concerted policy of ‘coordination’ (Gleichschaltung),” the U.S. Holocaust Memorial Museum writes. “Culture, the economy, education, and law all came under Nazi control.” Those artists and organizations that were not purged had their essential character changed to reflect an entirely different set of artistic and political values. One publication, especially, serves as an example of the Nazification of culture. The arts journal Jugend (Youth), writes Messy Nessy Chic, “had been turned largely into propaganda” between 1933 and 1940, its final year. But prior to the regime’s takeover, Jugend showcased the most avant-garde, “degenerate” artists of the era, and might have been “the ‘brainiest’ periodical of the day,” as one critic wrote in a 1904 issue of The Yale Literary Magazine. “There is no magazine published in England or in this country which is at all like it.” You can take a look yourself—browse, search, and download hundreds of scanned issues of Jugend at the University of Heidelberg’s digital archive, thousands of pages in PDF form, spanning the magazine’s forty-four-year history. You can also see images at Flickr. As in England, France, Austria, and the U.S., the Art Nouveau movement in Germany emerged from a whirlwind of post-Impressionist painting, Orientalist motifs, folk art, modernist art and advertising, book illustration, and graphic and industrial design. Appropriately, given its perch on the threshold of a new century, Art Nouveau looked both backward—to the medieval, gothic, and Romantic—and forward toward a more modernist, urbane, and urbanized sensibility. So influential was Jugend that Art Nouveau in Germany became known as Jugendstil. The Oxford Critical and Cultural History of Modernist Magazines writes, “Among Jugend’s most important qualities—indeed, an essential aspect of Art Nouveau and its German equivalent Jugendstil—was its brilliant escapism.” Founded in 1896 by writer Georg Hirth, the magazine was “from the start a venue to promote the new cultural Renaissance without recourse to the established ‘vintage’ art.” (See its very first cover right above.) cards.source_text: Frank Lloyd Wright was often strapped for cash. In that respect, he had something in common with Vincent van Gogh, who passed most of his much shorter life in more dire circumstances. Unlike Wright, who enjoyed decades of fame at the pinnacle of the American architectural profession, van Gogh remained practically unknown until after his death. But if they’ve encountered one another in the afterlife, they’ve certainly discussed one subject above all others: their shared appreciation for Japanese woodblock prints. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured the collection of 500 such works of art that van Gogh left behind. At the end of Wright’s life in 1959, he owned about 6,000, many of which his estate had to sell to pay both Japanese art dealers and American tax collectors. We could say that Wright died as he lived, advanced age having not evidently diminished either his financial recklessness or his obsession with ukiyo‑e. The masters of that classical “art of the floating world” like Hokusai and Hiroshige were among his favorite artists of any kind. When still a teenager, Wright went to work for the architect Joseph Silsbee, who’d built a chapel for his uncle. “Silsbee’s cousin, Ernest Fenollosa, happened to be the world’s leading Western expert on Japanese art at the time,” writes Kevin Nute at The Conversation. It isn’t certain how well the young Wright knew Fenollosa — or indeed when he began collecting ukiyo‑e, writes Frank Lloyd Wright and the Art of Japan author Julia Meech-Pekarik, though he may have seen both Hokusai and Hiroshige’s works at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago in 1893, “about the time he opened his practice in Oak Park.” Eight years later, “Wright made his first voyage to Japan in pursuit of prints, and he did indeed return with enough expertise to stage an exhibition of his own Hiroshige collection at the Art Institute of Chicago in March of 1906.” He returned for two months in 1913, making it clear that he was only interested in using that time to acquire more prints. Later, while working on the Imperial Hotel between 1917 and 1922, he spent a total of more than three years there, later writing that “the pursuit of the Japanese print became my constant recreation while in Tokio,” a quest whose “adventures and excursions would take place at night or sometimes call for a journey by day to distant places.” This positioned him well to take on a sideline as a dealer (or as he liked to call himself, a merchant) of Japan

In this video, Mary McGillivray, a digital creator and PhD student at the University of Melbourne, explores how, for as long as we’ve prized it, we’ve been inventing ways to fake it. cards.source_text: Just when you thought the kids had buried the Beatles for good, here’s AKRIILA with lucy miró al mundo y notó que está girando. The title of the rising Chilean star’s new album (“Lucy looked at the world and noticed it’s turning”) borrows lines from “While My Guitar Gently Weeps” and “Lucy in the Sky With Diamonds,” the first song AKRIILA learned to play on the piano. The Fab Four might seem like an unlikely reference point for a flame-haired 22-year-old whose berserk debut album was filled with robotic tags like “Hot gays listen to AKRIILA” and “Hot twinks listen to AKRIILA.” But the more you listen, the more it makes a weird kind of sense. AKRIILA makes omnivorous music, the byproduct of a peripatetic appetite and an inability or refusal to streamline her impulses. She doesn’t sound like the Beatles; she sounds like someone playing you her 10 favorite records at the same time, a charming mash of dog-eared pages and favorited tabs. Akri’s Lucy is not Julian Lennon’s classmate Lucy, nor LSD, nor a love interest. It's a protagonist learning to live alone in a grown-up, lovesick world—and also, separately, a snail. Snails are pathetic, precious things, locomoting calmly as chaos erupts around them. On the album cover, AKRIILA holds a snail named Lucy as light breaks in from every side. As lucy unfolds, the record moves from the bitter depths of heartbreak to something like acceptance, or the painful death that’s necessary for the light to eventually come back. On the trip-hoppy, dream-poppy second track, “moriría y moriría” (“I would die and die”), AKRIILA threatens to shoot herself if she can’t have her sweetheart. Fast forward to the languorous ache of closer “lucy,” where AKRIILA sees a snail that’s sure to die, and she gives up; she says the world has stopped turning. “Ya no sé por qué aún me esfuerzo,” (“I don’t know why I still try”), she sighs. No score yet, be the first to add. While the album is packed with these love-scarred lyrics and angsty entreaties, you wouldn’t know it from the production, which is mostly handled by longtime collaborators Heartgaze and Vinco. Where AKRIILA’s 2024 album epistolares turbocharged Nia Archives’ sensitive jungle for a neoperreo club night, lucy uses mad thuds and speedy rhythms sparingly, saving a “Think” break for a sick flash on “un <3 inestable.” The new sound is groovy guitars and drums that make being down bad sound like springtime bliss, like crying and smiling while watching the sunrise say hiii. cards.source_text: Hope Is the Thing With Feathers is a sort of homecoming for Rhiannon Giddens. The folk singer and string musician first gained acclaim for her work with the Carolina Chocolate Drops, a group dedicated to preserving traditional string band music of North Carolina. Since 2015, her solo career has taken her far afield, exploring the tributaries that flow from the folk music of the Carolinas: discovering austere, arty branches through her work with Italian multi-instrumentalist Francesco Turrisi and adding enough polish to her essential sound on 2023’s You’re the One so it resembled a crossover. A slight echo of You’re the One’s smooth assurance surfaces on her new record via “Carolina Rain.” The tune is broad and insistent enough to resemble a pop song, if only it was given a streamlined arrangement. Instead, “Carolina Rain” serves as a mile marker on an album that traces a path from Giddens’ folk beginnings through her worldly explorations and back home again. It’s a journey designed as a celebration, one that opens the door to include musicians from all corners of her career, ranging from regular collaborators Dirk Powell and Jason Sypher through Congolese guitarist Niwel Tsumbu to fiddle player Justin Robinson, with whom Giddens played in the Carolina Chocolate Drops. No score yet, be the first to add. Last year, Giddens reunited with Robinson for the joint record What Did the Blackbird Say to the Crow, a throwback to the impassioned traditionalism of their former band. Giddens brings that same enthusiasm to Hope Is the Thing With Feathers. The album flaunts frayed ends scattered throughout, like the studio chatter that precedes a raucous rendition of the folk standard “Old Cluck Hen.” These ragged accents make the music feel loose and alive—a touch of a mess that complements the clean yet earthy production of an album cut live in the studio. Similarly, Giddens varies her styles without calling attention to the breadth of material here. Original material written by her and Powell is balanced by folk tunes from a variety of sources, including interpretations of Elizabeth Cotten’s “Freight Train” and Ola Belle Reed’s “High on a Mountain,” a pair of songs associated with North Carolina. cards.source_text: When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, East Berlin crumbled. Many residents flocked to the West, compelled by the promise of a more robust economy and a higher standard of living. On the city’s eastern side lay a constellation of factories and industrial buildings, abandoned in the scramble of reunification. With curfews abolished and noise ordinances ignored, these neglected spaces became playhouses through the ’90s. At clubs and raves that enshrined techno, kink culture, and queer exploration, youthful mischief-makers gained access to their every unintelligible desire. In 2006, this is where Rhode Island native Gavilán Rayna Russom spawned Black Meteoric Star—before she joined LCD Soundsystem in 2008, before she came out as trans in 2017, and before she eventually left LCD to focus on work that felt truer to her. In the early aughts, Berlin was still a fleshy swirl of sonic freedom and sexual excess; jacking through electro, EBM, and freestyle, early Black Meteoric Star records reflected the erotic potential at her fingertips. Every rotten synthline and gravelly kick was a siren call to the dancefloor, directly inspired by her musings on dance music, drag, and the queer leather BDSM scene. The music’s trickster quality occasionally revealed glimpses of a life in deep transition—in Berlin, Russom was battling bouts of psychosis and traipsing through the concrete dens of the city after hours, emerging from techno-punctured darkness long after sunrise. No score yet, be the first to add. Today, Russom is back in the U.S., where she’s active as a DJ in the New York leatherdyke scene. Her latest album, Wet, which collects Black Meteoric Star tracks recorded as early as 2008, is a queer electro manifesto dripping in sex. “No amount of acting ‘respectable’ will humanize queer people in the eyes of this administration,” Russom writes in a press release. cards.source_text: Owen Williams wrote the last Tubs album, Cotton Crown, in the midst of a breakdown. But the harder you squint at their catalog, the harder it is to surmise what is breakdown and what is not. The Welsh singer’s unreliable narrators slip between gurning heartache and a self-sniping internal monologue that says cruel things you would never accept from a friend. His trade is failure anthems set to jangly folk-rock that stops short of storming the barn. Their darkest snapshots of tragedy and depression are often their funniest and winningest. On “Heaven or London” from their new record, Hard Life, Williams portrays himself as “the singer of a rip-off band” who is “wanking himself into an early grave,” playing “farm simulator,” and, for some reason, claiming to “write for The New York Times.” There is no tried-and-true path to success for a man like this, and it is unclear if Williams would take it. “I don’t wanna sell out this tour,” sings another of his narrators over duelling guitar and fiddle. “Don’t wanna play with the Tubs anymore/If you don’t love me.” The Tubs are the sort of band that has been down on its luck for so long that “down with luck” becomes its manifesto. The only thing for it is a crack at the small time: Write and record quickly, play gazillions of gigs, amble over to America, maybe briefly become the talk of the town. It helps to sign to one of the bigger indies; the new album is their Merge debut. But the uncertain journey ahead will be subject to chance, as well as a pathological fidelity to indie-pop principles: the DIY stance, the affinity for ruin, and the belief that love can make it all worthwhile but, knowing your luck, probably won’t. No score yet, be the first to add. Like many oddball bands operating in London, the Tubs’ longing for a dirtier, scrappier version of the city dovetails with a distaste for music likely to make much money. It is hard to disentangle their romantic fatalism from their tech-ravaged industry and dire social conditions. The rewards of a rich artistic life come to those who remain open to the world, which can be hard when paying a fortune for a crap apartment well into your thirties. Money helps, as does delirious self-belief. The Tubs, like so many bloody-minded artists living 40 to 50 years too late, appear to have scant hope of either. The rest of the band, for all their ramshackle fervor, barely put up a fight against Williams’ defeatist lyrics. Lead guitarist Dan Lucas is new to the fold—George Nichol

cards.source_text: Curbside Lambsear means nothing. As a band name, it’s drawn from a photo Magdalena McLean posted on Instagram a few years ago—of a lamb’s-ear plant that was growing next to a curb—and does not really necessitate interrogation. But wow, what a phrase to say out loud! There’s no band I’d rather speak the name of right now: Those consonant clusters give the tongue a real workout, bring back Proustian memories of spelling bees and schoolyard riddles. When I say Curbside Lambsear are wordy, I don’t mean in a literal sense. Maybe I’d describe them as wordsy: as in, headsy about words. Just listen to the title of their debut EP: Put Rings on All My Fingers to Weigh Down My Hands. The construction practically encourages you to swing it as you say it out loud: Put Rings on-All-My Fingers to Weigh Down My Hands. McLean and her bandmate Annabelle Mödlinger say they write lyrics together, phrase by phrase, meaning their songs don’t contain full narratives; what they lack in discrete stories they more than make up for in structural beauty. When one of them intones that “No ordinary word makes the world fit right into the palms of me/No ordinary word makes the world makes the world makes the world,” I have no idea what they might be referring to—but it’s easy to lurch into the pessimistic beauty of the whole thing. No score yet, be the first to add. Viola player McLean and synth player Mödlinger were both born in Austria, but became friends in London as members of sparky art-rock band the Umlauts. McLean also performs in Caroline as a violinist and co-vocalist, and an understanding of that band is helpful in parsing the aesthetic world of Curbside Lambsear, which similarly manages to blend elements of drone and noise into a world that still feels pretty and pastoral. Most frequently, Curbside Lambsear’s music recalls the work of Tirzah and Mica Levi in its willingness to find grooves in harsh environs (as on “Avril”) or to contrast sweet, almost childlike vocal takes with dubby, decaying production (“Uneasy”). items.title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from?
items.summary: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The Power In his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schubert’s favourite pupils. This, Wittgenstein argues, was a totally understandable act of grief. He goes on to suggest, however, that if, in his grief, Schubert’s brother had left the scores untouched, or even burned them, then that too would be equally legible to us. Such is the disorienting nature of loss – in its wake, anything goes. In The Strangers, Women’s prize-winning author Naomi Alderman tests this thesis to its limits. How about dealing with grief by writing an uneasy memoir/speculative fiction hybrid about the sudden appearance of a new species of quasi-badgers that seem to improve the quality of local soil?
